Radio-Imaging Examina- Tion Methods Of The Musculoskeletal System

Carolina Solomon

11.1. Conventional radiography (X-ray)

Represents the fifirst-line radio-imaging method for evaluating bone and joint pathology, especially in post­traumatic conditions. The most important reason is that it is cheap, non­invasive and painless, but, unfortunately, irradiating.

Examination technique:

  • it is mandatory to perform two or­< thogonal incidences;

  • the two adjacent joints for each bone< segment must be included;

  • standard radiography is performed< in anteroposterior (AP) and lateral­lateral (LL, profifile) incidence (fifigure 69);

    Fig. 69. Comparative X-ray of the knees (R for

  • it is recommended to perform com­ parative radiographs in the case of paired bone segments;
  • it is indicated to perform radiographs with hard rays and overvoltage, respectively, with soft rays to visualize bone structure changes or those of soft parts;
  • sometimes additional views are ne­ eded:
  • oblique;
  • enlarged radiographs are used to re­ veal bone details and to multiply the information provided by a radiogra­ phic image;
  • the stress incidences are extremely useful for assessing ligament inju­ ries and joint stability (for example,< r right): a) AP view; b) profifile view of the right knee. 96 l II. THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM

X­ray examination allows the assessment of bone morphology:

  • evaluation of the cortex and bone< marrow, as well as the joint space;

  • epiphyseal, metaphyseal and diaphy­< seal regions;

  • joint alignment;
  • recognition of bone and joint lesions,< as well as establishing the radiological diagnosis Conventional radiography is an irra­< diating technique. It is contraindicated in pregnant women. Since irradiation increases with the number of exposures, the risk of carcinogenic lesions increases with repeated exposures.

    11.2. Computed Tomography (CT)

    There are several benefifits to CT scans:

  • This imaging method represents a< fast, non­invasive, painless one;

  • CT obtains images in the transverse< plane, with the subsequent possibility of reconstructing them in the sagittal, coronal and oblique plane, and multiplanar/ three­dimensional reconstructions, being an indispensable method in evaluating traumatic pathology and bone and soft tissue tumors;

  • The CT examination accuracy is< higher than that of conventional X­ray in the diagnosis, follow­up, and guidance of diagnostic or therapeutic interventional maneuvers;

  • CT examination provides valuable< information about joint congruence, bone structure, and tissues structure around the bone and joint;

  • CT examination shows much higher< contrast resolution and accuracy in measuring the tissue attenuation coeffificient compared to conventional radiography;

  • CT examination accurately assesses< the extent of bone damage, disruption of the bone cortex and damage to surrounding soft tissues, including those located in complex anatomical bone structures, such as the scapula, pelvis, or sacrum, challenging to assess on X­ray examination fully Tumor staging, post­therapy evalua­< tion, and diagnosis of recurrences are performed using CT examination;

  • The administration of contrast me­< dia increases the accuracy of the radiological diagnosis by visualizing intratumoral vascularization. This examination can also identify inapparent lesions on native images;

  • Last but not least, CT examination< reveals the status of bone mineralization (fifigure 70).

    Disadvantages:

    CT examination shows an increased degree of irradiation, the dose being higher than that of the X­ray examination.

    Also, in the case of the contrast agent’s administration, its contraindications must be taken into account (see the chapter on contrast agents).

    11.3. Arthrography

    This investigation method consists of introducing the contrast agent (positive iodinated substance, negative ­ air, or mixed ­ the combination of the two) into the joint space.

    Arthrography is available both by the conventional method and by CT or MRI techniques.

    Arthrography is especially useful in the diagnosis of:

  • injuries of the rotator cuff or< the adhesive capsulitis at the level of the shoulder joint;

  • dissecting osteochondritis, osteo­< chondral bodies and changes of the cartilage in the elbow joint;

  • changesinthetriangularfifibrocartilage< at the level of the radio­carpal region. ODS OF THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM l 97

    11.4. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

    MRI is a non­irradiating, non­invasive and painless imaging technique. It is used to evaluate all diseases of the musculoskeletal system, mainly for the diagnosis of trauma, arthritis, tumors and infections.

    In this method, the acquisition of images is obtained in all three planes: axial, sagittal and coronal, which allows the detailed study of the examined area (fifigure 71).

    Usefulness of MRI examination:

  • MRI is the only imaging method that identififies the medullary signal, highlighting bone edema;
  • The method provides important information about the status of the carti­ lage and joint space;
  • The accuracy of the diagnosis of soft tissue lesions (muscle, tendon, liga­ ment, vascular­nervous, subcutaneous

Fig. 71. Saggital T1 weighted MR image of the spine. 98 l II. THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM cellular tissue) is high in the case of MRI examination;

  • It represents the optimal method for< assessing the early stages of rheumatoid arthritis, sacroiliitis or other inflflammatory/ autoimmune diseases with musculoskeletal involvement;

  • MRI examination is the fifirst-line< method in spinal cord injuries or cases with clinical examination suggestive of signifificant acute spinal cord compression, with severe neurological defificits (e.g., paresis, urinary retention) There are two options for performing< MRI arthrography: direct, by intra­articular injection of gadolinium­based contrast agent; respectively indirectly, by its intravenous injection The longer examination time com­< pared to other radiological methods and the contraindications specifific to the method represent the disadvantages of MRI examination in the case of exploration of the musculoskeletal system.

    11.5. Ultrasound (US)

    US is an accessible, non­irradiant, repeatable imaging method, easy to use whenever needed and relatively inexpensive to examine the musculoskeletal structures.

    Ultrasound examination helps highlight changes in muscle, tendon, ligament

    Fig. 72. Longitudinal panoramic US scan of t and the meniscus, synovial, subcutaneous cell tissue and vascular­nervous structures (fifigure 72).

    Ultrasound is used to accurately diagnose several diseases of the musculoskeletal system, including:

  • tendon injuries;
  • soft tissue lesions;
  • rheumatic diseases, with particular importance in highlighting the presence of intra- and periarticular flfluid, as well as hypertrophied synovia;
  • rotator cuff injuries;
  • differentiation of the flfluid or paren- chymal nature of a lesion;
  • evaluation of intra­ or perilesional vascularization;
  • differentiating vascular pathology from the rheumatic one (for example, the differential diagnosis of Baker cyst vs. popliteal artery aneurysm vs. deep venous thrombosis of the popliteal vein or deep venous axis of the calf).

Considering that US examination can be performed from birth, it represents the imaging method of choice to assess hip joint in newborns, infants and children. It is also indicated as a screening method for the diagnosis of hip dysplasia.

In clinical practice, a series of interventional maneuvers can be performed under ultrasound guidance: intraarticular diagnostic and therapeutic punctures; muscle or tumor biopsies. the arm.

11. RADIO-IMAGING EXAMINATION METHO

One of the disadvantages of this imaging method is that it has low accuracy in assessing bone lesions. Operator dependence is also a disadvantage to consider in the case of ultrasonographic examination of the musculoskeletal system.

Radiologic Anatomy Of The Bones

Manuela Lenghel

2.1. Descriptive anatomy

2.1.1. Histology.

The normal bone contains bony tissue, bone marrow, vessels and nerves. The periosteum surrounds the bone.

The bone tissue is a connective tissue composed of the matrix and bone cells.

1. The matrix consists of an organic matrix (20-40%) and inorganic mineral salts (50-70%). The organic matrix is formed mainly by collagenous proteins (85-90%), especially collagen fifibers type 1. The non-collagenous proteins represent only 10-15%, with an essential role in bone mineralization adjustment and bone cell proliferation. The inorganic salts consist predominantly of phosphate and calcium ions, forming the hydroxyapatite crystals. The association of these components is responsible for bone stiffness and resistance.

2. The bone cells are divided into: a. Osteoblasts – the bone­forming cells deri­

ved from the mesenchymal line; b. Osteocytes – the mature bone cells, located

within lacunae, surrounded by mine­

ralized bone matrix, with a dendritic

morphology. Osteocytes play an im­

portant role in bone support and are

involved in the metabolic activity;

c. Osteoclasts – are differentiated multinucleated cells derived from the macrophage­mononuclear cells, with a bone resorption role.

The structure of the bone tissue is

different according to the degree of tissue maturity.

1. The adult bone tissue. According to cells, fifibers and bone matrix disposition, it is divided into:

a. compact bone tissue presents a lamellar disposition of the bone matrix, with a central channel (Havers) surrounded by concentric blades formed by the bone matrix. The Havers channel contains blood vessels, nerves and a small quantity of bone marrow. An anastomosis exists between neighboring systems, with opening in the medullary cavity and under the periosteum. The osteocytes found in the bone or between the bone lamella communicate through the bone canaliculus dendrites. The compact bone tissue’s morphofunctional unit is the osteon (the Haversian system) formed by the concentric lamellar system, Havers canal and bone cells. Compact bone tissue is present in the diaphysis of the long bones.

b. cancellous bone tissue is formed by irregular, widened cavities, delineated by the cortical bone; the cavity walls are

12 formed by thin bone blades, oriented in all directions.

2. Immature bone tissue is represented by a heterogeneous and very irregular distribution of the matrix (collagen fifibers) and bone cells. It is characteristic for the newborn and the fifirst year of life.

2.1.2. Classification of the bones

1. Long bones are located in the peripheral skeleton, in the limbs. The length is the highest dimension and they present three different parts: the diaphysis, which represents the body of the bone and the epiphysis, the extremity of the bone. The connection between the central part of the bone and the periphery is the metaphysis. The diameter of the epiphysis is higher compared with the diaphysis and metaphysis.

2. Plane bones. The length and the width are the highest dimensions, almost equal in size. Skull base and scapula are some examples.

3. Short bones. All three dimensions are almost equal in size (vertebral body, carpal and tarsal bones).

2.1.3. Bone growth and remodeling

The process of bone formation is called osteogenesis. It is divided into:

1. Primary osteogenesis – resulting in an immature, incomplete bone that appears after the connective and cartilaginous tissue change into bone tissue.

2. Secondary osteogenesis – is responsible for adult bone formation secondary to bone destruction and remodeling.

Fibrous (membranous) osteogenesis (encountered in the skull base and facial bones) consists of membranous tissue metaplasia due to ossifification points formation. The osteogenesis evolves from the center towards the periphery, with bone 2. RADIOLOGIC ANATOMY OF THE BONES l 101 growth. The bone maturation appears after the osteoclasts’ activation.

Cartilaginous (enchondral) osteogenesis consists of the replacement of cartilaginous tissue by bone tissue. The mechanisms encountered are peripheral, periosteal or perichondral osteogenesis and central (enchondral) osteogenesis.

The bone maturation:

1. Osteoresorbtion appears secondary to osteoclasts activity, with cavity formation. It is activated by parathormone, vitamin A and cortisone.

2. Osteoformation is due to osteoblast activity, with organic matrix secretion. After the mineralization, the osteoblast is transformed into an osteocyte. Factors favoring osteoformation are GH, insulin, vitamin C, androgens, estrogens and calcitonin.

The mineralization degree is inflfluenced by phosphate and calcium salts, vitamin D, malabsorption, renal pathologies, hyperemia, stasis, pH.

2.2. Imaging of the joints

1. Synarthrosis (immobile joints) example: sacroiliac joint. CT and MRI are the methods of choice for the evaluation, with optimal assessment of the bone structure and joint space.

2. Amphiarthrosis (partially mobile joints) ­ example: spine joints. MRI is the method of choice to evaluate the medullar canal, ligaments and intervertebral disk. CT is associated for assessing bone structure changes.

3. Diarthrosis (mobile, synovial joints) ­ example: elbow, knee. Besides CT and MRI, US and conventional x­ray play an important role in assessing these joints. 102 l II. THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM

2.3. Radiologic anatomy

2.3.1. The radiologic appearance of the adult bone

The compact bone delineates the periphery of the long bones’ diaphysis and appears opaque on conventional X­ray. Towards the epiphysis, it becomes thinner and forms the cortical bone. The central part of the diaphysis is transparent and represents the medullary canal. The nutrient canal with the vessels and the nerves supplying the bone is located in the middle of the diaphysis and appears as a thin transparent line. The cancellous bone is found in the epiphysis, presenting a less opaque aspect and a more lax structure. The articular cartilage is not generally detected on X­ray. (fifigure 73).

Fig. 73. Comparative AP radiograph of the forearms. The typical appearance of the long bones is depicted. For details see text.

The periosteum contains vascularized connective tissue surrounding the bone, except the joint surfaces. Normal periosteum in inapparent on X­ray or CT.

The short bone contains spongy tissue. Cortical bone is found in the periphery.

Like the short bone, the plane bone presents cancellous tissue in the center, surrounded by the cortical bone.

Ultrasound is benefificial in assessing the soft tissues. The cortical bone has a hyperechoic appearance, sharp contour except the areas corresponding to the nutrient canal, enthesis, tubercles and epicondyles. Due to acoustic shadowing, the analysis of the deep part of the bone is, practically, impossible.

On CT, the medullar canal is usually hypodense and the cortical bone presents high density, up to + 1000 HU, representing the highest density among the normal structures of the human body.

On MRI, the cortical bone is hypointense in all sequences. The bone marrow presents an inhomogeneous signal, with hyperintense appearance on T1 and T2 for fat and intermediate T2 signal and hyperintense aspect on T1 for the hematogenous marrow.

2.3.2. The radiological aspect of the joint

The joint spaces between the bone surfaces are transparent on X­ray, showing uniform width (fifigure 74). US and MRI are the methods of choice to assess the joint spaces and intra­ and extraarticular small parts. The dynamic examination is an advantage of US. MRI also detects bone changes.

Ultrasound and MRI are the imaging methods of choice for the evaluation of the joints due to their excellent resolution and providing exact anatomical and pathological details of the intra­ and extraarticular

12

Fig. 74. Comparative AP radiograph of the kn structures: cartilage, joint capsule, synovia, joint space, tendons and ligaments, subchondral bone changes and the neighboring bursae. Ultrasound has many advantages regarding the costs, availability, being a non­irradiating and noninvasive technique. Another main advantage is the dynamic assessment of the musculoskeletal structures.

The cartilage surrounds the joint surface. On MRI, it usually appears hypointense on T1 and presents intermediate signal on T2. Ultrasonography detects a hypoechoic linear structure with a homogenous appearance.

The joint capsule presents a low signal on T1 and T2 sequences, with hyperechoic linear appearance on US.

The synovial flfluid is anechoic on US and has the typical appearance on MRI T1 and T2 sequences.

The ligaments and tendons present a marked hypointensity on T1 and T2 2. RADIOLOGIC ANATOMY OF THE BONES l 103 nees. Typical appearance of diarthroses. sequences due to protons’ reduced content. In US, a fifibrilar pattern with increased echogenicity is typical for normal ligaments and tendons. There are a few exceptions, however: the cruciate ligaments (anterior and posterior) are hypoechoic, diffificult to assess and the medial collateral ligament has a three­layered appearance.

2.3.3. The radiologic appearance of the immature bone and joint

The growth plate is present during childhood. It appears as a transparent line located between the epiphysis and diaphysis. It is delineated by the temporary ossifying line towards the diaphysis. The epiphysis presents an opaque nucleus, surrounded by a radiotransparent cartilage. The bony apophyses are separated from the rest of the bone body. The joints appear wider due to incomplete development and ossifification of the components (fifigure 75). 104 l II. THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM

Musculoskeletal Semiology

Dan Vasilescu, Sorin M

Abnormalities of the musculoskeletal system may involve the bones, the muscles or the tendons.

13.1. Bone changes

Bone changes may affect the bone as an organ or they may involve the bone tissue.

13.1.1. Alterations of the bone as an organ 13.1.1.1. Alterations in size

Congenital:

Agenesis – bone absence from the birth;

Hypoplasia – bone smaller than normal;

Hyperplasia – bone larger than normal;

Acquired:

Anostosis – failure of bone formation (ossifification) or atrophy of bone;

Hypostosis – defificient development of bone resulting in a thinner bone/bone segment;

Hyperostosis – an excessive growth of bone resulting in a thicker bone/bone segment (fifigure 76).

13.1.1.2. Alterations of the shape

Blown-out – oedostosis, distended contour of the affected bone, “balloon” like appearance, the compact layer being M. Dudea intact ( as in aneurysmal bone cyst) (fifigure 77);

Bone scoliosis – curved bone appearance, similar to the spine’s curvatures visible in the frontal plane, scoliosis (fifigure 78).

Fig. 76. Hyperostosis of the left tibia. Chronic osteomyelitis.

Kyphosis – posterior convex curvature of the spine, visible in the sagittal plane;

Lordosis – anterior convex curvature of the spine, visible in the sagittal plane.

13.1.2. Alterations of the bone tissue

They may be destructive, productive or necrosis.

13.1.2.1. Destructive

1. Osteoporosis is defifined as the reduction of bone mineral density without losing protein matrix. In terms of skeletal damage expansion, there are three major forms:

a) Generalized osteoporosis affects the whole skeleton. The most common causes are post­menopausal and senile status. Until the 8th decade, the condition is more common in females who also have an earlier onset in the 6th decade. In the initial phases, the symptoms are absent. They appear simultaneously with the complications due to bone resistance reduction: fractures caused by minor traumas, alterations in the vertebrae conformation followed by secondary vertebral static disorders.

Conventional radiography is not used for diagnostic purposes of osteoporosis but may show specifific changes represented by:

  • Increased bone transparency is the< defifining sign for osteoporosis due to the reduction of bone density by at least 30% (osteopenia) (fifigure 79)

  • Decrease of the cortico­diaphyseal< ratio – visible at the le;vel of long bones, due to the thinning of the compact bone with the implicit widening of the medullary canal

  • Alteration of the cancellous bone< architecture by resorption of some trabeculae and hypertrophy of those oriented along the direction of stress forces (e.g., bodyweight) (fifigures 80, 81).

    13.1.2.2. Productive

    This type of fundamental change implies the production of additional bone tissue in the form of osteosclerosis, periostosis or ossifification and heterotopic bone production.

    1. Osteosclerosis can be considered, from a certain point of view, the opposite of osteoporosis. Radiologically, the osteosclerotic lesion appears more opaque due

3. Ossifications and heterotopic calcifications

a) Osteophytes are bone productions around the joints, with the initial direction perpendicular to the originating bone surface. When large, the base is thick, and the tip often curves toward the joint space. Osteophytes are characteristic of degenerative joint disease, osteoarthritis (fifigure 89).

b) Sindesmophytes are thin bone productions located at the spine’s level on the external portion of the intervertebral disc. Their origin is in the corner of a vertebra; their direction is vertical, from one vertebra to another, which they often join, producing ankylosis. They are characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis (fifigure 90).

13.1.2.3 Osteonecrosis

It can be produced by two primary mechanisms that defifine the two types: infectious – septic and ischemic ­ aseptic.

1. Septic osteonecrosis occurs in bone infections, namely osteomyelitis. The typical lesion in osteomyelitis is bone sequestrum. It appears as an opaque bone fragment surrounded by an osteolytic area. The surrounding bone tissue reacts by delimiting the area of osteolysis through an island of osteosclerosis, with an irregular, geographical map-like shape (fifigure 91). All these features, although radiographically visible, are best highlighted by CT.

2. Aseptic osteonecrosis typically occurs in the spongy bone of the epiphyses or short bones. It is due to vascular disorders that lead to blood supply interruption. As a result, there are initial areas of osteoporosis and osteolysis, bands of osteosclerosis, and then fragmentation and collapse

13.2 Muscle changes

Ultrasound is the fifirst choice imaging method to assess muscle structures. The US has multiple advantages: easily accessible, cheap, non­irradiant and real­time. It provides a high­resolution assessment of superfificial structures. Diffificulties occur when the targeted muscle structures are deeply located.

Muscle fifibers appear as hypoechoic bands in US. They are wrapped in the perimysium, which appears as a fifine hyperechoic line. Muscle fascias also appear as hyperechoic structures. The muscle orientation and fifibrillar architecture are best seen in the longitudinal scans when the appearance is comb­like. In cross­sections, the aspect is roughly punctuated by an alternation of hypo­ and hyperechoic dots (fifigure 93).

Muscle hypertrophy translates into dimensional growth of the muscle. Due to muscle fifibers volume increase, the overall muscular appearance is hypoechoic.

Muscle hypotrophy implies overall dimensional reduction, with decreased muscle fifibers, fatty infifiltration and an accentuated fifibrous appearance. Therefore the global US aspect will be of increased echogenicity.

13. MUSCULOSKELETAL SEMIOLOGY l 115

CT scan shows muscles having an intermediate density, but it is not the method of choice to assess muscle disease.

MRI is the most effificient method for evaluating muscle pathology, having the ability to visualize the target structure’s global structure. Typical muscle structures have a hypointense appearance.

13.3. Tendon changes

As in the case of muscles, the tendons are evaluated fifirst with ultrasound. They mostly contain collagen fifibers that produce a parallel fifibrillar hyperechoic ultrasound appearance (fifigure 94). In cross-section, the aspect is rounded or oval, fifine dotted and hyperechoic. The echogenicity is higher than that of muscles.

The tendons may be wrapped in the peritendon or the synovial sheath.

The peritendon has the appearance of a hyperechoic cover and is found in the supraspinatus, Achilles, patellar and quadriceps tendons. For easier sliding, these tendons are accompanied by bursae.

The synovial sheath is a thin 0.1-0.2 mm structure that appears hypoechoic, surrounding the fifibrillar tendon. It is seen in long biceps, flflexor digitorum and extensor carpi tendons.

The insertion of the tendon on the bone surface is called enthesis and has a uniform structure. The diseased state of an enthesis is named enthesopathy.

On CT scans, tendons are seen as intermediate density structures.

MRI shows tendons with low signal intensity.
